description_full: Capri Holdings Limited engages in the design, marketing, distribution, and retail of branded women's and men's apparel, footwear, and accessories in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and the Oceania. It operates through two segments: Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo. The company offers handbags, small leather goods, jewelry, scarves and belts, and footwear and related accessories through a distribution network, including retail stores, department and specialty stores, and licenses to wholesale customers, as well as e-commerce sites. It also undertakes licensing agreements relating to manufacture and sale of watches, jewelry, eyewear, and fragrances. The company was formerly known as Michael Kors Holdings Limited and changed its name to Capri Holdings Limited in December 2018. Capri Holdings Limited was founded in 1981 and is based in London, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: Capri Holdings Limited is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.2B market cap on $3.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -15% over the past three years and -3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $14M in free cash flow — roughly 0 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.56×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.9% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
